title: How fast? The rate of chemical change
summary: Reaction rate depends on the frequency of successful collisions. Explain the effects of concentration, temperature, surface area and catalysts with collision theory and Maxwell–Boltzmann curves; at HL, rate equations, mechanisms and the Arrhenius equation.

keyterms.definition: Change in concentration of a reactant or product per unit time, in mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹.
Reactions occur when particles collide with the correct orientation and at least the activation energy.
The minimum energy colliding particles need for a reaction to occur.
Curve showing the number of particles with each kinetic energy at a given temperature; area under it = total particles.
A substance that increases rate by providing an alternative pathway with lower Ea, and is regenerated at the end.
Exposed area of a solid reactant; increasing it (smaller pieces) increases collision frequency.
Rate = k[A]ᵐ[B]ⁿ; orders m and n are found by experiment, not from the equation.
The power to which a concentration is raised in the rate equation; overall order is the sum.
Proportionality constant in the rate equation; it changes with temperature and its units depend on overall order.
The slowest step in a reaction mechanism; species in it appear in the rate equation.
The number of particles reacting in an elementary step (unimolecular, bimolecular).
k = Ae^(−Ea/RT); a plot of ln k against 1/T has gradient −Ea/R.

lessons.title: Collision theory and factors affecting rate

questions.prompt: Why does increasing concentration increase rate?
questions.explanation: More particles per unit volume collide more often, so there are more successful collisions per second.

questions.statement: Raising temperature increases rate mainly because a greater proportion of collisions have energy ≥ Ea.
questions.explanation: Collision frequency also rises slightly, but the bigger effect is more particles exceeding Ea.

questions.prompt: How does a catalyst increase rate?
options: It shifts the Maxwell–Boltzmann curve to the right
It provides an alternative pathway with lower activation energy
questions.explanation: More particles then have energy ≥ the lower Ea. The distribution itself is unchanged.

questions.text: At a higher temperature, the peak of the Maxwell–Boltzmann curve moves to the right and becomes ___.
questions.explanation: The area (total number of particles) is constant, so the curve flattens as it spreads.

questions.prompt: Match each change to its main effect.

pairs.right: Larger surface area, more frequent collisions

questions.explanation: Always link a factor to collision frequency or to the fraction with E ≥ Ea.

questions.statement: A catalyst changes the enthalpy change of the reaction.
questions.explanation: ΔH depends only on reactants and products; a catalyst changes only the pathway.

questions.prompt: Marble chips react with HCl and the mass of the flask is recorded. Why does the mass fall?
questions.explanation: CaCO₃ + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂; the escaping gas lowers the mass, which tracks the rate.

questions.text: The rate at a given time is found from the ___ of a concentration–time graph.
questions.explanation: Draw a tangent at that time; rate = |gradient|.

questions.prompt: Order the conditions from slowest to fastest initial rate (same mass of zinc, excess acid).
questions.explanation: Each change adds a factor that increases successful collision frequency.

questions.prompt: Why is the rate fastest at the start of a reaction?
questions.explanation: As reactants are used up, collisions become less frequent and rate decreases.

questions.prompt: Rate = k[A]²[B]. If [A] is doubled and [B] is halved, the rate…

questions.text: For rate = k[NO]²[O₂], the overall order is ___.
questions.explanation: Overall order = 2 + 1 = 3.

questions.statement: Orders of reaction can be read from the coefficients of the overall balanced equation.
questions.explanation: Orders come from experiment; they reflect the rate-determining step, not the overall equation.

questions.prompt: What are the units of k for a second-order reaction?
questions.explanation: k = rate / [ ]² → (mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹)/(mol dm⁻³)² = dm³ mol⁻¹ s⁻¹.

questions.prompt: Match each order to its concentration–time or rate graph.
questions.explanation: For first order, rate–[A] is a straight line through the origin.

questions.prompt: A two-step mechanism: step 1 (slow) NO₂ + NO₂ → NO₃ + NO; step 2 (fast) NO₃ + CO → NO₂ + CO₂. The rate equation is…
questions.explanation: Only species in (or before) the slow step appear: rate = k[NO₂]². CO is zero order.

questions.statement: The rate constant k increases with temperature.
questions.explanation: From k = Ae^(−Ea/RT), higher T gives a larger k.

questions.text: A plot of ln k against 1/T has gradient equal to ___.
questions.explanation: ln k = ln A − Ea/(RT); the intercept is ln A.

questions.prompt: Order the steps to find Ea from rate data at several temperatures.
items: Convert temperatures to K and calculate 1/T
questions.explanation: Units: with R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹, Ea comes out in J mol⁻¹.
Molecularity counts the particles in an elementary step; termolecular steps are rare.
